cards.explanation: The answer is rejoice and let your heart be glad. The Teacher, a king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says, "Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth." Notice he opens with gladness, friends. I've heard plenty of advice in my day, and a king telling you to be glad is the kind I'd frame on the bakery wall.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, "Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment." Right after all that gladness comes a quiet "but know." He lets the young man enjoy the road and still tells him plainly that God will bring him to judgment.

The answer is fleeting. The Teacher says, "So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are fleeting." Vigor means strength, and he's saying it doesn't stay. It's like a fresh cookie on the cooling rack at my place, friends. It looks like it will be there forever, and then I turn around.

The answer is the days of adversity. The Teacher says, "Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come…" He puts the remembering first and the hard days after. A smart baker preheats the oven before the dough is ready, and this is the same idea.

The answer is "I find no pleasure in them." The Teacher says "…the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). That's what a person says about those years. It's a heavy line, so I'll just say it plainly: I think it's meant to make us listen.
The answer is False. The verse says, "…before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain…" The clouds come back. That's a gray picture, friends.
The answer is False. The verse says the keepers of the house tremble "…and the strong men stoop…" The strong men are bent over. Even the strong ones in this picture are bowing low, friends.

The answer is because they are few. The verse says, "…when those grinding cease because they are few…" The work stops because those grinding are few. It's like a bakery shift where everybody went home and left me alone with the mixer. Wait, I'm alone with the mixer every day.
The answer is the sound of a bird. The verse says "…when one rises at the sound of a bird…" In the Teacher's picture, that's the sound a person rises at. Just a bird, friends, and up the person goes.

The answer is False. The verse says, "…when men fear the heights and dangers of the road…" Nobody is bolder here, friends. They fear the heights and the dangers of the road. I think we all know a ladder that looks taller than it did last year.
The answer is to his eternal home. The verse says "…for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets." The Teacher says it quietly and plainly. It's a heavy line, friends.

The answer is that each one gets broken. The silver cord is "snapped," the golden bowl is "crushed," the pitcher is "shattered" and the wheel is "broken" (Ecclesiastes 12:6). Four different things, and each one is broken. That's the thread running through the whole verse.

The answers are ground and God. The verse says "…before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it." The dust goes back to where it came from, and the one who gave the spirit is the one it returns to. This is a quiet, heavy line, friends, and I'll leave it that way.

The answer is True. The last line of the passage says, "“Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher. “Everything is futile!”" It's a hard thing to end on, and it comes right after the Teacher's pictures of the dust and the spirit (Ecclesiastes 12:7). I think it's worth sitting with for a second, friends.
